briefs.what: In April 1861, with Southern states in armed rebellion and Congress not in session, President Lincoln proclaimed a naval blockade of Confederate ports. Union ships captured merchant vessels and cargoes trying to run it, and the lower courts condemned them as prizes of war. The owners argued that only Congress can declare war, and since it hadn’t, there could be no lawful blockade and no lawful capture.
briefs.ruling: When war is forced on the nation, the President “does not initiate the war, but is bound to accept the challenge without waiting for any special legislative authority.” Whether the rebellion amounted to a war was his call, which the courts would follow, and Congress later removed any doubt by ratifying his orders.

briefs.what: Lambdin Milligan, an Indiana citizen who had never served in the military, was arrested at home in 1864 on Army orders for plotting with a secret society to overthrow the government, free prisoners, and seize weapons. A military commission convicted him and sentenced him to hang, even though the federal court in Indianapolis was open and its grand jury never indicted him. He petitioned for habeas.
briefs.ruling: Because Indiana’s courts were open and no fighting was there, the military had no power to try a civilian: “Martial rule can never exist where the courts are open.” Five Justices said even Congress could not authorize such a trial, while four (led by Chief Justice Chase) agreed only because Congress hadn’t.

briefs.what: Costanzo, an Italian citizen who had lived in the U.S. for more than five years, was arrested, given a hearing, and ordered deported for managing a house of prostitution. He argued in habeas that the 1917 Immigration Act allowed deportation on that ground only within five years of entry. The lower courts dismissed his petition.
briefs.ruling: The five-year limit belonged only to the clause it appeared in, so he could be deported on this ground at any time. Because Congress had left the statute alone despite the agency’s consistent reading, its inaction created “a presumption in favor of the administrative interpretation.”

briefs.shortTitle: United States v. Curtiss-Wright Export Corp. (1936)
briefs.what: In 1934 Congress passed a joint resolution letting the President ban arms sales to Bolivia and Paraguay, then at war in the Chaco, if he found a ban would help restore peace, and he issued one that day. Curtiss-Wright and others were indicted for conspiring to sell fifteen machine guns to Bolivia. The trial court dismissed the charge, holding that Congress had unconstitutionally handed its lawmaking power to the President.
briefs.ruling: The delegation was valid because Congress may give the President far more discretion in foreign affairs than at home. Sutherland rooted this in “the very delicate, plenary and exclusive power of the President as the sole organ” in international relations, a power that needs no act of Congress but must still obey the Constitution.

briefs.what: In June 1942, eight German-trained saboteurs came ashore by submarine on Long Island and in Florida, buried their uniforms and explosives, and moved inland in civilian clothes to attack U.S. war industries. After the FBI caught them, President Roosevelt ordered a military commission to try them for violating the law of war. Seven petitioned for habeas, including Herbert Haupt, who claimed U.S. citizenship.
briefs.ruling: Enemy fighters who slip in out of uniform to attack are unlawful belligerents, and Congress had authorized military commissions to try them, so Milligan did not apply. Citizenship would not save them, because it “does not relieve him from the consequences of a belligerency which is unlawful.”

briefs.shortTitle: Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer (1952)
briefs.what: During the Korean War, a nationwide steel strike was set for April 1952, and President Truman believed it would cripple weapons production. Hours before the strike began, he ordered the Commerce Secretary to seize and run most of the nation’s steel mills, relying on no statute, only his general powers as President and Commander in Chief. Congress, which had refused to authorize such seizures in the Taft-Hartley Act, did nothing, and the steel companies sued.
briefs.ruling: No statute allowed the seizure, and the President’s executive and military powers do not let him make domestic law, so the order was void. Justice Jackson’s concurrence supplied the test courts now use: presidential power is at its “maximum” when Congress authorizes it, uncertain in a “zone of twilight” when Congress is silent, and at its “lowest ebb” when he defies Congress.

briefs.what: Eldridge was receiving Social Security disability benefits when a state agency, reviewing his medical reports and written answers, decided his disability had ended. The government cut off his payments without first holding an evidentiary hearing, although he could get one afterward and receive full back pay if he won. He sued, and the lower courts held that due process required a hearing before termination.
briefs.ruling: No pre-termination hearing was required, because written procedures were reliable enough for a medical question and he could be made whole later. The Court set the test for how much process is due, which balances three factors: (1) the private interest at stake, (2) the risk of error under the current procedures and the value of added safeguards, and (3) the government’s interest, including the burden those safeguards would impose.

briefs.what: Yaser Hamdi, an American citizen born in Louisiana, was captured in Afghanistan in 2001 and handed to the U.S. military, which says he fought for the Taliban. He was held at Guantanamo, then moved to a Navy brig in the U.S. once the government learned he was a citizen. Calling him an “enemy combatant,” the government claimed it could hold him indefinitely with no charges, no lawyer, and no hearing, so his father filed for habeas.
briefs.ruling: Congress’s AUMF lets the President detain someone captured fighting for the Taliban, but only for the length of the conflict and never just to interrogate him. Even so, a citizen who disputes the label gets notice of the facts against him and “a fair opportunity to rebut the Government’s factual assertions before a neutral decisionmaker.”

briefs.what: Nyynkpao Banyee, a citizen of Ivory Coast who grew up in the U.S. as a lawful permanent resident, was placed in removal proceedings after a string of crimes ending in a conviction for robbery with a dangerous weapon. Federal law required that he be held without bond while his case went back and forth for about a year. The district court found that too long, ordered a bond hearing, and he was released.
briefs.ruling: The Eighth Circuit reversed, holding that “[d]ue process imposes no time limit on detention pending deportation,” as long as removal is still possible and the proceedings aren’t a pretext. It rejected a case-by-case reasonableness test, reasoning that the Supreme Court had already done the Mathews balancing for this kind of detention.

cases.title: The Prize Cases, 67 U.S. (2 Black) 635 (1863)
cases.meta: The Court decided the case 5–4. Justice Grier wrote the majority opinion. Justice Nelson dissented, joined by Chief Justice Taney and Justices Catron and Clifford (at 699). The case appears at pages 635–699 of the packet and relates to Issue 2.
cases.Facts: In April 1861, with Southern states in armed rebellion, President Lincoln ordered a naval blockade of Confederate ports before Congress met in special session (at 666, 675; Nelson, J., dissenting, at 695). Union ships captured four merchant vessels and their cargoes, which belonged to Richmond residents and to Mexican and British shippers (at 674–82; Nelson, J., dissenting, at 682). District courts in Massachusetts, New York, and Florida ruled that the ships and cargo were lawful prizes of war, and the owners appealed to the Supreme Court (at 674–80).
cases.Question: Could the President lawfully blockade Southern ports before Congress had declared or recognized a war (at 665, 668)?
cases.Holding: Yes. When war is made on the nation, the President must respond with force without waiting for Congress, and courts accept his judgment that a war exists (at 668–70). The Court added that even if congressional approval were required, Congress gave it when it later passed a law approving Lincoln's orders (at 670–71). Property belonging to anyone living in Confederate territory could be captured regardless of the owner's personal loyalty (at 674). The Court upheld nearly all of the captures but returned one New York firm's tobacco (at 675–82).
cases.Reasoning: The Constitution gives Congress alone the power to declare war. It also makes the President Commander in Chief, and federal laws passed in 1795 and 1807 allowed him to use the military against invasion and insurrection (at 668). A civil war does not need a formal declaration. It exists when rebels hold territory, raise armies, and begin fighting, or when the courts cannot stay open (at 666–67). The Confederacy met that standard, and Britain had already recognized the conflict as a war (at 669). The Court limited its own ruling in two ways: the President cannot start a war (at 668), and doubts about a claimant's case are resolved in the claimant's favor (at 675).
cases.Dissent: Justice Nelson argued that a war in the legal sense exists only when Congress declares or recognizes it, so every capture made before Congress acted in July 1861 was void (at 689–90, 698–99). He also wrote that the President cannot turn a loyal citizen into an enemy (at 695). The dissent spoke for four Justices and is not law.
cases.Government:
* The President may act against a threat without waiting for Congress, and courts accept his judgment about how much force the threat requires (quotes 1–3).
* Congress has supported the President here through the AUMF and NDAA § 1021, just as it approved Lincoln's orders in 1861 (quote 4).
* Whether someone is treated as an enemy depends on his conduct and connections, not his citizenship (at 674).
cases.Bronner:
* The Court relied on federal statutes and on Congress's later approval, not on presidential power alone (at 668, 670–71). Here, Congress limited offshore detention to people unlawfully present in the country (ATA § 4(b)(1)) rather than approving the President's order.
* The case concerned ships captured at sea during an active war, not a lawful resident arrested at home while the courts were open and had released him on bond (quote 6).
* Even in wartime, each claim was decided in court, and doubts were resolved for the claimant (quote 7). Bronner has had no comparable hearing on the sealed evidence against him.
quotes: "He does not initiate the war, but is bound to accept the challenge without waiting for any special legislative authority." (at 668)
"The President was bound to meet it in the shape it presented itself, without waiting for Congress to baptize it with a name" (at 669; quoted by the Fourteenth Circuit majority, R. at 11)
"this Court must be governed by the decisions and acts of the political department of the Government to which this power was entrusted." (at 670)
"this ratification has operated to perfectly cure the defect." (at 671)
"He has no power to initiate or declare a war either against a foreign nation or a domestic State." (at 668)
"so that the Courts of Justice cannot be kept open, civil war exists" (at 667)
"All reasonable doubts should be resolved in favor of the claimants." (at 675)
"Certainly it cannot rightfully be said that the President has the power to convert a loyal citizen into a belligerent enemy" (at 695, Nelson, J., dissenting)

cases.title: Ex parte Milligan, 71 U.S. (4 Wall.) 2 (1866)
cases.meta: All nine Justices agreed on the judgment, which was entered at the end of the prior term. Justice Davis wrote the opinion of the Court for five Justices. Chief Justice Chase concurred, joined by Justices Wayne, Swayne, and Miller. The arguments of counsel (at 9–106) are not part of the opinion.
cases.Facts: In 1863, Congress authorized the President to suspend habeas corpus. The same statute required that prisoners not indicted by the next grand jury be discharged. Lambdin Milligan was a citizen who had lived in Indiana for twenty years and had never served in the military or lived in a rebel state (118). He was arrested at his home on October 5, 1864, on a general’s order and held in a military prison. A military commission tried him on five charges, including conspiracy, aiding rebels, and violating the laws of war. The specifications accused him of communicating with the enemy and plotting to seize munitions and free prisoners of war . He was sentenced to hang, and the President approved the sentence (107). A federal grand jury met in Indianapolis from January 2 to 27, 1865, and did not indict him (at 107–08). He petitioned the Circuit Court to be turned over to the civil courts or discharged. The two judges disagreed and certified three questions to the Supreme Court (108–09).
cases.Question: Did the military commission have legal authority to try and sentence Milligan (at 118)?
cases.Holding: No. Milligan should be discharged under the 1863 Act, and the commission had no jurisdiction (at 107). The laws of war cannot be applied to civilians in loyal states where the courts are open (at 121), and Congress could not grant that power (at 122). Martial rule is allowed only where the courts are actually closed, and only in the area of actual war (at 127). Separately, the 1863 Act entitled Milligan to release because the grand jury did not indict him (at 115–16, 131).
cases.Reasoning:
A trial is an exercise of judicial power. The Constitution gives that power to Article III courts. The commission was not a court created by Congress, and the President’s order could not make it one (at 121). Congress had already made Milligan’s alleged conduct a federal crime and given the Indiana court power to try it. Those courts were open and working, so nothing made a military trial necessary (at 122).
The Constitution applies in war as well as in peace (at 120–21). In a rebellion or invasion, suspending the writ lets the government arrest and hold people without producing them in court. But the Constitution “goes no further”: suspension does not permit a military trial (at 125–26). Martial law requires a real and present necessity, not a threatened invasion. It lasts only as long as the necessity does (at 127).
Milligan was not a prisoner of war. He lived in Indiana, was arrested there, and had not taken part in lawful acts of war. Since he could not claim a prisoner of war’s protections, he could not be subjected to its penalties (at 131). Congress allowed the President to detain people in 1863, but only for a fixed period unless a court proceeding began (at 115). Its plain purpose was to guarantee release when the courts found no grounds to charge (at 116).
cases.Concurrence: Chief Justice Chase agreed that the 1863 Act alone decided the case (at 136). He disagreed that Congress lacked the power to authorize military commissions where courts are open. In his view, Congress had that power but had not used it (at 136–37). He found that Congress had instead implicitly forbidden such trials in Indiana (at 141). He also wrote that the military, even when operating abroad, cannot exceed the President’s authority or the laws Congress passes (at 141). He described three kinds of military jurisdiction (at 141–42).
cases.Government:
* Milligan is about a military trial, not detention. Bronner has not been tried. The Court itself accepted that a dangerous person may be arrested and held without trial in an emergency. It said suspected plotters may be held “until the government was prepared for their trial.” That is the government’s position: it will try him “as soon as practicable” (IC 7).
* Milligan depended on his not being a combatant (at 118, 131.
   * Quirin read Milligan’s laws-of-war language as limited to “the facts before it.” 
   * The Executive has classified Bronner as an unprivileged enemy belligerent for materially supporting hostilities (App. II § 948a(7)(B)).
* Congress has authorized detention here.
   * Four Justices said Congress may authorize military process (quote 13), and Quirin limited the majority’s broader statement.
   * Congress acted through AUMF § 2(a) and NDAA § 1021(c)(1) (IC at 12; App. III).
   * The 1863 Act limited the President; these statutes grant him power.
* The necessity is real. Arranging to buy a dirty bomb (IC at 6, 11) is an actual and present danger, not a “threatened invasion.” The government should rest on Bronner’s conduct, not on where he was arrested; it cannot claim he was captured on a battlefield.
cases.Bronner:
* The courts were open, and they already had him. The District of Olympus arraigned him, set bond, and had a pending material-support felony carrying up to 20 years (IC at 7 & n.7). Quote 4 maps onto this almost exactly: why was he not left with the court that already had his case? The dissent makes this point (IC at 17–18).
* The Fourteenth Circuit misreads Milligan. It describes Milligan as not supporting enemy forces (IC at 12). But Milligan was charged with communicating with the enemy and plotting to seize munitions (IC at 6–7), and the Court still treated him as a civilian. Combatant status depends on what is proven, not on what is alleged. The Attorney General reclassified Bronner based on an accusation alone (IC at 7).
* The President made new law. Executive Order 15000 reaches non-citizens “regardless of immigration status” (IC at 3), which ATA § 4(b)(1) does not allow. Under quote 2, the President executes the law; he does not write it.
* Even the concurrence favors Bronner. The concurrence requires Congress to act, and treats a limiting statute as an implied prohibition. ATA § 4(b)(1)–(2) and the rejected bills (IC at 3) play the role the 1863 Act played. Moving him to Guantanamo does not escape that limit.
* Emergency detention has to end. Congress’s own Civil War model required a fixed period followed by court process. Bronner has been held 12 months on sealed evidence with no end date (IC at 6–7).
quotes: “The Constitution of the United States is a law for rulers and people, equally in war and in peace, and covers with the shield of its protection all classes of men, at all times, and under all circumstances.” (at 120–21)
“They cannot justify on the mandate of the President; because he is controlled by law, and has his appropriate sphere of duty, which is to execute, not to make, the laws” (at 121)
“they can never be applied to citizens in states which have upheld the authority of the government, and where the courts are open and their process unobstructed.” (at 121)
“Why was he not delivered to the Circuit Court of Indiana to be proceeded against according to law?” (at 122)
“Martial law cannot arise from a threatened invasion. The necessity must be actual and present” (at 127)
“Martial rule can never exist where the courts are open, and in the proper and unobstructed exercise of their jurisdiction.” (at 127)
“As necessity creates the rule, so it limits its duration” (at 127)
“If any of her citizens were plotting treason, the power of arrest could secure them, until the government was prepared for their trial, when the courts were open and ready to try them.” (at 127)
“the peril to the country may be too imminent to suffer such persons to go at large” (at 125)
“The Constitution goes no further. It does not say after a writ of habeas corpus is denied a citizen, that he shall be tried otherwise than by the course of the common law” (at 126)

“it was not contemplated that such person should be detained in custody beyond a certain fixed period, unless certain judicial proceedings, known to the common law, were commenced against him.” (at 115)
“If he cannot enjoy the immunities attaching to the character of a prisoner of war, how can he be subject to their pains and penalties?” (at 131)
“We think that Congress had power, though not exercised, to authorize the military commission which was held in Indiana.” (at 137, Chase, C.J., concurring)
“That body did not see fit to authorize trials by military commission in Indiana, but by the strongest implication prohibited them.” (at 141, Chase, C.J., concurring)
“wherever our army or navy may go beyond our territorial limits, neither can go beyond the authority of the President or the legislation of Congress.” (at 141, Chase, C.J., concurring)

cases.title: Costanzo v. Tillinghast, 287 U.S. 341 (1932)
cases.meta: Justice Roberts wrote for the Court. The case came on certiorari to the First Circuit and was decided December 5, 1932. The opinion text notes no separate opinions.
cases.Facts: Section 19 of the Immigration Act of 1917 required the deportation of any alien who managed a house of prostitution. Costanzo, a citizen of Italy, was arrested, given a hearing, and ordered deported on that ground. He petitioned for habeas. The District Court dismissed the writ, and the First Circuit affirmed (at 342). He had entered the country "much more than five years" before the arrest warrant issued (at 343). He abandoned his constitutional claim below (at 342).
cases.Question: Section 19 opens with the phrase "at any time within five years after entry." Does that phrase limit every deportable class listed in the section, or only the class in its own clause (at 343)?
cases.Holding: It limits only its own clause. No limitation period applies to this ground, so the alien may be taken into custody and deported at any time after entry (at 343–45). The judgment was affirmed. Separately, where the Secretary of Labor's order is supported by evidence, a habeas court will not review his findings (at 342–43).
cases.Reasoning:
* Structure. Section 19 is a single sentence of nearly 900 words. It contains eleven subject clauses that share one predicate (at 343). Three of those clauses carry their own time terms, and seven carry none, including Costanzo's. The five-year phrase therefore cannot govern all of them, and it belongs only to its own clause (at 344).
* Syntax yields to intent. Punctuation is not decisive (at 344).
* No surplusage. The third proviso makes the section apply "irrespective of the time of their entry." If the five-year limit carried over to every clause, the proviso would have nothing to do (at 344–45).
* History. The earlier statutes covering this class contained no time limit (at 345).
* Acquiescence. The Bureau's rules had read § 19 this way uniformly since 1917, across successive editions (at 345 & n.3). Congress failed to amend the section despite that consistent reading, which creates a presumption in favor of it (at 345).
cases.Government:
* Inaction means acquiescence. Presidents have asserted the power to detain unprivileged enemy belligerents “regardless of their citizenship,” and Congress repeatedly declined to forbid it (IC at 2–3). Under Costanzo, that failure to act gets “great weight” even if the Court doubts the reading (at 345). The majority relies on this (IC at 12), and EO 15,000 invokes it (IC at 24).
* Limits stay in their own clause. The only location limit in the ATA applies to citizens (§ 4(b)(2)). Like § 19’s time limits, it shouldn’t be carried over to other groups. Section 4(a) reaches “any person who is present in the United States” (IC at 23).
* Intent over grammar. Read § 4 in light of the Act’s purpose and § 3(a)’s “vast, expansive” finding (IC at 22).
* Residence is no shield. Costanzo was deportable long after entry (at 343).
* Deference. Habeas courts do not reweigh executive findings that are supported by evidence (at 342–43).
cases.Bronner:
* No departmental construction. Costanzo’s presumption rested on an agency’s consistent reading of its own statute over years of rules (at 345 & n.3). Here the ATA, the PAT, and Bronner’s reclassification all date to 2025. Presidential claims of inherent power are not a construction of statutory text.
* Congress acted. It enacted § 1022(b)(2), § 1021(e), and ATA § 4(b), and it rejected offshore detention of citizens. A pending bill to authorize offshore detention of lawful non-citizens shows Congress thinks that power doesn’t yet exist (IC at 3, 20–23).
* Whole-statute reading. Section 4(b)’s only offshore grant runs to persons “unlawfully present.” If § 4(a) already permitted offshore detention of anyone, that clause would have “nothing upon which [it] may operate” (at 344).
* Deference presupposes process. Costanzo deferred to findings made after a hearing and on evidence (at 342–43). Bronner got neither, which makes this a bridge to Hamdi.
* Wrong field. Costanzo is a deportation case about statutory construction. It says nothing about Article II or military detention (at 342).
quotes: "we should not apply the rules of syntax to defeat the evident legislative intent." (at 344)
"There is nothing upon which this proviso may operate if such of the preceding clauses as contain no time limitation are qualified by the Words of the first" (at 344)
"We must look to the whole of the section, in order not to give undue effect to particular words or clauses" (at 345)

"The failure of Congress to alter or amend the section, notwithstanding this consistent construction by the department charged with its enforcement, creates a presumption in favor of the administrative interpretation, to which we should give great weight, even if we doubted the correctness of the ruling of the Department of Labor." (at 345)
"The petitioner, a citizen of Italy, was arrested, given a hearing, and ordered deported" (at 342)

cases.title: United States v. Curtiss-Wright Export Corp., 299 U.S. 304 (1936)
cases.meta: Justice Sutherland wrote for the Court. Justice McReynolds dissented without opinion; he would have affirmed (at 333). Justice Stone took no part.
cases.Facts: A Joint Resolution of May 28, 1934, made it a crime to sell arms to countries fighting in the Chaco if the President found that a ban "may contribute to the reestablishment of peace" and so proclaimed. The ban lasted "until otherwise ordered by the President or by Congress" (at 312). President Roosevelt issued the proclamation the same day and revoked it November 14, 1935 (at 312–13). Curtiss-Wright and others were indicted for conspiring to sell fifteen machine guns to Bolivia (at 311). The District Court sustained their demurrer, holding the Resolution an unlawful delegation of legislative power, and the government appealed directly (at 314).
cases.Question: Is the Joint Resolution an unconstitutional delegation of legislative power to the President, given that it concerns foreign affairs (at 315)?
cases.Holding:
No. The Court reversed (at 329, 333). It also held that (1) the President's finding was sufficient because it followed the Resolution's language (at 331); and (2) revoking the proclamation did not end liability for offenses already committed (at 331–32).
The Court expressly reserved whether the same delegation would be valid if it concerned internal affairs (at 315).
cases.Reasoning:
* Two kinds of power. The rule of enumerated powers is "categorically true only in respect of our internal affairs" (at 315–16). External sovereignty passed from the Crown to the Union as a whole, not to the states (at 316–17). It "did not depend upon the affirmative grants of the Constitution" (at 318). The power to expel undesirable aliens is part of that external sovereignty (at 318).
* Sole organ. In the external realm, "the President alone has the power to speak or listen as a representative of the nation" (at 319).
* Discretion and secrecy. The President has confidential sources, and premature disclosure can cause harm (at 320). Statutes operating in the international field may therefore give him freedom "which would not be admissible were domestic affairs alone involved" (at 320).
* Historical practice. An unbroken legislative practice since 1794 of giving the President broad foreign-affairs discretion carries "unusual weight" (at 322, 327–29).
* The President cannot repeal a statute. Only Congress can end the Resolution's force (at 331–32).
cases.Government:
* Inherent power. The President's foreign-affairs power "does not require as a basis for its exercise an act of Congress" (at 320). Terrorism tied to foreign arms dealers is an external threat, and the PAT targets "foreign-enabled" activity.
* Statute plus inherent power. As in Curtiss-Wright, the President acts on a statute and his own power (at 319–20). That is Youngstown Category 1, and the majority relies on this (IC at 11–12).
* Broad discretion is expected. Foreign-affairs statutes need not set "narrowly definite standards" (at 321–22). The ATA's presidential-finding trigger for offshore detention works like the Resolution's finding trigger.
* Sealed evidence is defensible. Secrecy over intelligence sources is "highly necessary" (at 320), which justifies keeping the dirty-bomb documents sealed.
* Aliens fall within external sovereignty. The power to expel undesirable aliens is inherent in nationality (at 318). Bronner is not a citizen.
cases.Bronner:
* The holding is narrow. Curtiss-Wright decided a delegation question. The President acted on an "exertion of legislative power" plus his own (at 319–20). The "sole organ" language is dictum, and nothing in the case upholds the President acting without a statute.
* The internal/external line cuts for Bronner. The Resolution's "whole aim" was "entirely external" (at 315), and the Court reserved the domestic question. Arresting a 30-year resident in his home state and holding him is an internal matter. Curtiss-Wright explains why its reasoning does not reach this case.
* The Constitution still applies. Even plenary power is exercised "in subordination to the applicable provisions of the Constitution" (at 320). That opens the way to Hamdi and Mathews.
* The President cannot override a statute. "Congress alone" controls a statute's force (at 332). ATA § 4(b)(1) limits offshore detention to persons unlawfully present. An executive order reaching people "regardless of immigration status" effectively repeals that limit.
* A valid finding must track the statute. The proclamation survived because it "follows its language" (at 331). The AG's "removable non-citizen" classification does not track § 4(b)(1)'s "unlawfully present" requirement.
* The secrecy passage is about diplomacy. It concerns negotiation papers withheld from the House (at 320–21), not evidence used to imprison a person. Curtiss-Wright itself was enforced through an indictment in an open court.
quotes: "the investment of the federal government with the powers of external sovereignty did not depend upon the affirmative grants of the Constitution." (at 318)
"The President is the sole organ of the nation in its external relations, and its sole representative with foreign nations." (at 319, quoting Marshall)

"the very delicate, plenary and exclusive power of the President as the sole organ of the federal government in the field of international relations—a power which does not require as a basis for its exercise an act of Congress, but which, of course, like every other governmental power, must be exercised in subordination to the applicable provisions of the Constitution." (at 319–20)
"Secrecy in respect of information gathered by them may be highly necessary, and the premature disclosure of it productive of harmful results." (at 320)
"It was not within the power of the President to repeal the Joint Resolution" (at 331)
"No action or lack of action on the part of the President could destroy its potentiality. Congress alone could do that." (at 332)

cases.title: Ex parte Quirin, 317 U.S. 1 (1942)
cases.meta: Chief Justice Stone wrote for the Court. The Court issued a per curiam decision on July 31, 1942, and filed the full opinion October 29, 1942. Justice Murphy took no part.
cases.Facts:
All eight petitioners were born in Germany and had lived in the United States (at 20). Haupt claimed U.S. citizenship through his parents’ naturalization; the government said he had renounced it. The Court did not resolve the question (at 20).
After war was declared, the petitioners trained at a German sabotage school. German submarines then landed them at night on Long Island and in Florida, wearing German uniforms or uniform caps and carrying explosives (at 21). They buried their uniforms and moved inland in civilian dress. The German High Command had paid them and instructed them to destroy American war industries (at 21–22). FBI agents arrested them in New York and Chicago (at 21).
By Order, the President convened a military commission. By Proclamation, he subjected enemy saboteurs to military tribunals and denied them access to the courts (at 22–23). The FBI then surrendered the petitioners to military custody (at 23). The commission convened July 8 and had closed the evidence by July 27 (at 23). The government conceded that the civil courts were “open and functioning normally” throughout (at 23–24).
cases.Question: Was the petitioners’ detention for trial by military commission consistent with the Constitution and the laws of the United States (at 18–19)?
cases.Holding: Yes. The charge alleged an offense against the law of war that the President was authorized to try by commission. The commission was lawfully constituted, and the petitioners were in lawful custody (at 48). The Court denied leave to file the habeas petitions and affirmed the District Court.
cases.Reasoning:
* Courts may still hear the case. The Proclamation could not bar the courts from deciding whether it applied to these men, or whether the Constitution forbade their trial (at 25).
* Congress had acted. Through Article of War 15, Congress authorized military commissions to try law-of-war offenses. The President acted on that statutory authority together with his own powers as Commander in Chief (at 26–28). The Court therefore did not decide whether he could create commissions without Congress (at 29).
* Lawful vs. unlawful combatants. Both may be captured and detained. Unlawful combatants may also be tried for the acts that make their belligerency unlawful (at 30–31). Discarding the uniform after entering U.S. territory makes an enemy agent an unlawful belligerent (at 35–37).
* Citizenship is irrelevant to belligerent status. A citizen who joins the enemy’s military arm is an enemy belligerent (at 37–38). The offense was complete on entry with hostile purpose, even without an attack or presence in a combat zone (at 38).
* No jury right. Law-of-war offenses were never triable by jury as of right (at 38–45).
* Milligan distinguished. Milligan’s language was tied to “the facts before it.” Milligan was not associated with the enemy’s armed forces (at 45).
* Narrow holding. “We hold only that those particular acts constitute an offense against the law of war” (at 46). The Court also left open whether Congress may restrict the Commander in Chief’s power over enemy belligerents (at 47).
cases.Government:
* Detention is a war power. Unlawful combatants may be captured and detained (at 31). If citizenship does not shield a belligerent (at 37), lawful permanent residence cannot. The majority below relies on this (IC at 11).
* Open courts don’t control. The courts were open in Quirin too (at 23–24), and Milligan is limited to its facts (at 45). Quirin also followed the same sequence as this case: FBI arrest, then transfer to the military (at 21, 23).
* No battlefield required. The offense is complete on hostile entry. The target need not be the armed forces, and the hostile act need not be completed (at 37–38). That fits a planned dirty-bomb purchase.
* Statute plus inherent power. As with Article 15, Congress authorized military action here, now through the AUMF and NDAA (at 28–29).
* Deference. War-time detention is not to be set aside without a “clear conviction” that it is unlawful (at 25).
cases.Bronner:
* Quirin was about trial, and a fast one. The men were “held in good faith for trial” (at 46), and the evidence closed within three weeks of the commission convening (at 23). Bronner has waited over a year with no trial and no tribunal.
* Status rested on conceded facts. The admitted facts showed the charge was not “merely colorable” (at 36, 46). Bronner denies the allegations, and the evidence is sealed.
* Enemy belligerency required an enemy military. The saboteurs were in uniform, under the German High Command, and delivered by submarine during a declared war (at 21–22, 37–38). Suspected ties to arms dealers are not association with an enemy armed force.
* The holding is narrow. The Court said “We hold only” (at 46). It did not decide whether the President has inherent power without Congress (at 29) or whether Congress may limit him (at 47). Quirin supports the government only if Congress actually authorized this detention.
* Courts retain review. Even a Proclamation barring access to the courts could not prevent judicial review (at 25).
quotes: “there is certainly nothing in the Proclamation to preclude access to the courts for determining its applicability to the particular case.” (at 25)
“Constitutional safeguards for the protection of all who are charged with offenses are not to be disregarded in order to inflict merited punishment on some who are guilty.” (at 25)

“It is unnecessary for present purposes to determine to what extent the President as Commander in Chief has constitutional power to create military commissions without the support of Congressional legislation.” (at 29)
“Unlawful combatants are likewise subject to capture and detention, but in addition they are subject to trial and punishment by military tribunals” (at 31)
“Citizenship in the United States of an enemy belligerent does not relieve him from the consequences of a belligerency which is unlawful” (at 37)
“We construe the Court’s statement ... as having particular reference to the facts before it.” (at 45)
“upon the conceded facts, were plainly within those boundaries, and were held in good faith for trial by military commission” (at 46)

cases.title: Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer, 343 U.S. 579 (1952)
cases.meta: The vote was 6–3. Justice Black wrote for the Court, and Justices Frankfurter, Douglas, Jackson, and Burton joined him and wrote separately. Justice Clark concurred only in the judgment. Chief Justice Vinson dissented, joined by Justices Reed and Minton.
cases.Facts:
In late 1951 the steelworkers' union threatened a strike. The President referred the dispute to the Wage Stabilization Board, but no settlement followed (at 582–83). The union then called a nationwide strike for April 9, 1952.
Hours before the strike, President Truman issued Executive Order 10340, directing the Secretary of Commerce to seize and operate most of the nation's steel mills (at 583). He relied on no statute, invoking only his powers under the Constitution and as Commander in Chief (at 585). He reported the seizure to Congress twice, and Congress did nothing (at 583).
The District Court enjoined the seizure, and the Court of Appeals stayed the injunction. The Supreme Court granted certiorari within days (at 584).
cases.Question: Was the seizure within the President's constitutional power (at 582)?
cases.Holding:
No. The order "cannot stand" (at 589). The District Court's injunction was affirmed.
Majority (Black)
* Two possible sources. The President's power "must stem either from an act of Congress or from the Constitution itself" (at 585). No statute authorized the seizure. In 1947 Congress had specifically rejected seizure as a way to settle labor disputes (at 586).
* Commander in Chief. Even though "theater of war" is an expanding concept, the Commander in Chief cannot seize private property to keep labor disputes from stopping production. "This is a job for the Nation's lawmakers, not for its military authorities" (at 587).
* Take Care. The duty to execute the laws "refutes the idea that he is to be a lawmaker" (at 587). The order executed a presidential policy, in a manner the President chose (at 588).
* Past practice. Prior presidential seizures do not strip Congress of its lawmaking power (at 588–89).
Concurrences
Frankfurter (at 593–614)
* Narrow scope. He deliberately set aside what the President could do if there were no relevant legislation, or if a seizure were "short, explicitly temporary," and ended automatically without congressional approval (at 597).
* Congress's pattern. Congress granted seizure power at least 16 times, "uniformly" for a limited period or a defined emergency (at 597–98).
* Withholding counts as a prohibition. In 1947 Congress withheld seizure power "as though it had said so in so many words" (at 602). Where Congress specifically addressed a problem, a court cannot find "secreted in the interstices of legislation the very grant of power which Congress consciously withheld" (at 609).
* Need is not authority. The absence of presidential authority does not mean the Government lacks power. "The need for new legislation does not enact it" (at 603–04).
* Historical gloss. "A systematic, unbroken, executive practice, long pursued to the knowledge of the Congress and never before questioned" may be treated as a gloss on the "executive Power" (at 610–11). He gave an example of 252 withdrawals over 80 years. By contrast, three isolated 1941 seizures were not enough and lacked "long-continued acquiescence of Congress" (at 611, 613).
Douglas (at 629–34)
* Emergency is only an occasion. "The emergency did not create power; it merely marked an occasion when power should be exercised" (at 629).
* Compensation. A seizure is a taking. Only the branch that can pay compensation, which is Congress, can authorize one (at 631–32).
* Military vs. civilian. Our history "rebel[s] at the thought that the grant of military power carries with it authority over civilian affairs" (at 632).
* Take Care. The power to execute "starts and ends with the laws Congress has enacted" (at 633).
* Footnote. Lincoln suspended habeas corpus, and Congress later ratified the suspension (at 631 n.1).
Jackson (at 634–55)
* Powers fluctuate. Presidential powers "are not fixed but fluctuate, depending upon their disjunction or conjunction with those of Congress" (at 635).
* Category 1: authorization. When the President acts with express or implied authorization from Congress, his power is at its maximum. His action gets "the strongest of presumptions and the widest latitude of judicial interpretation" (at 635–37).
* Category 2: twilight. When Congress has neither granted nor denied authority, the President acts in a "zone of twilight." Congressional "inertia, indifference or quiescence" may, at least practically, invite independent presidential action (at 637).
* Category 3: lowest ebb. When the President acts against Congress's expressed or implied will, his power is at its lowest. Courts can uphold him only by "disabling the Congress from acting upon the subject" (at 637–38).
* Applying the categories. Category 1 was eliminated by concession. Category 2 was eliminated because Congress had "covered" the field with inconsistent statutory policies (at 638–39). That left Category 3.
* On Curtiss-Wright. That case involved the President acting "under and in accord with an Act of Congress." Much of the opinion is dictum. It intimated that the President might act without Congress, "but not that he might act contrary to an Act of Congress" (at 636 n.2).
* War power turned inward. A President cannot enlarge his "mastery over the internal affairs of the country by his own commitment of the Nation's armed forces to some foreign venture" (at 642). He is not "Commander in Chief of the country, its industries and its inhabitants" (at 643–44).
* Outward vs. inward. Jackson would give the "widest latitude" when national force is turned against the outside world, but not when it is turned inward over a lawful economic struggle (at 645). It is "not a military prerogative, without support of law, to seize persons or property" (at 646).
* Take Care vs. Due Process. The Take Care Clause reaches "so far as there is law." The Due Process Clause guarantees "that authority shall go no farther" (at 646).
* Emergency power. The Constitution's only express emergency provision is habeas suspension (at 650). Emergency powers are safe only when "their control is lodged elsewhere than in the Executive who exercises them" (at 652). Unchecked, "such power either has no beginning or it has no end" (at 653).
Burton (at 655–60)
* Congress reserved seizure. Taft-Hartley's omission of seizure power was deliberate, and Congress reserved that remedy for itself (at 657, 660).
* What he left open. He distinguished an "imminent invasion or threatened attack." The Court did not face what the President's power would be in "such catastrophic situations" (at 659).
Clark, concurring in the judgment (at 660–67)
* Congressional procedures control. Where Congress has laid down specific procedures for a type of crisis, the President must follow them (at 662).
* Otherwise, gravity decides. Absent such procedures, his independent power depends on "the gravity of the situation" (at 662).
* The analogy he relied on. In a case Clark described, a statute authorized seizure of vessels sailing to French ports. That limited grant implicitly excluded seizure of vessels sailing from them (at 660–61).
Dissent (Vinson, joined by Reed and Minton) (at 667–710)
* Extraordinary times. He stressed Korea and the defense program (at 668–72). The majority's view leaves the President "powerless at the very moment when the need for action may be most pressing" (at 680).
* Limited and temporary. Truman's action was temporary, reported to Congress immediately, and subject to Congress's will. It was meant to preserve the status quo "until Congress could act" (at 701, 703, 710).
* No prohibition. No statute prohibited seizure (at 703).
cases.Government:
* Category 1 applies. The AUMF and NDAA § 1021 authorize detention, so the President acts with "the strongest of presumptions" (at 637).
* At worst, Category 2. Congress repeatedly declined to bar this detention, and that inertia "invite[s]" independent action (at 637).
* Youngstown reserves this case. Jackson gives the widest latitude to force turned outward (at 645). Burton set aside a "threatened attack" (at 659), and Clark recognizes power proportioned to "gravity" (at 662). A planned dirty-bomb purchase is not a "lawful economic struggle."
* Historical gloss. Successive Presidents have asserted this detention power with Congress's knowledge (at 610–11).
* No statute forbids it. Unlike Taft-Hartley's rejection of seizure, the ATA is silent on lawful residents (IC at 3).
cases.Bronner:
* Category 3 applies. Congress addressed the field through ATA § 4(b), § 1022(b)(2), and its rejected bills. Under Frankfurter, withheld power cannot be found "in the interstices" (at 609). Under Clark, a specific limit excludes everything outside it (at 660–62).
* Persons, not just property. Jackson's language reaches detention directly: "seize persons" (at 646). The President is not Commander in Chief of the country's "inhabitants" (at 644), and a foreign war cannot enlarge his internal power (at 642).
* Curtiss-Wright is limited. Jackson's footnote confines it to action consistent with an Act of Congress (at 636 n.2).
* Even the dissent's case is different. Frankfurter reserved only short, explicitly temporary action (at 597). The dissent rested on temporariness and deference to Congress (at 701, 710). Bronner's detention is open-ended.
quotes: "When the President acts pursuant to an express or implied authorization of Congress, his authority is at its maximum" (at 635, Jackson, J.)
"congressional inertia, indifference or quiescence may sometimes, at least as a practical matter, enable, if not invite, measures on independent presidential responsibility." (at 637, Jackson, J.)
"Presidential claim to a power at once so conclusive and preclusive must be scrutinized with caution" (at 638, Jackson, J.)
"it is not a military prerogative, without support of law, to seize persons or property" (at 646, Jackson, J.)
"The need for new legislation does not enact it." (at 604, Frankfurter, J.)
"where Congress has laid down specific procedures to deal with the type of crisis confronting the President, he must follow those procedures" (at 662, Clark, J.)

cases.title: Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319 (1976)
cases.meta: Justice Powell wrote for six Justices. Justice Brennan dissented, joined by Justice Marshall. Justice Stevens took no part. The Court decided the case February 24, 1976.
cases.Facts:
Eldridge began receiving Social Security disability benefits in 1968 (at 323). In 1972 the state agency sent him a questionnaire and obtained reports from his physician and a psychiatric consultant. It then sent him a tentative determination that his disability had ended, with a statement of reasons and an invitation to submit more information (at 323–24). He disputed one finding in writing. The agency finalized its decision, and the Social Security Administration terminated his benefits (at 324).
Instead of seeking reconsideration, Eldridge sued. He claimed due process required an evidentiary hearing before his benefits were cut off (at 324–25). The District Court agreed, and the Fourth Circuit affirmed (at 326).
cases.Question: Does the Due Process Clause require an evidentiary hearing before disability benefits are terminated (at 323)?
cases.Holding:
No. The existing procedures "fully comport with due process" (at 349). The judgment was reversed.
On jurisdiction, the Court held that a claim to pre-deprivation process is "collateral." It may be heard without full exhaustion, because full relief cannot come after the fact (at 330–32).
cases.Reasoning:
* The baseline. Some form of hearing is required before a final deprivation. The core requirement is the opportunity to be heard "at a meaningful time and in a meaningful manner" (at 333).
* Flexibility. Due process "is flexible and calls for such procedural protections as the particular situation demands" (at 334).
* The three factors (at 335):
   1. the private interest affected;
   2. the risk of erroneous deprivation under the existing procedures, and the probable value of additional safeguards;
   3. the Government's interest, "including the function involved" and the burdens of added procedures.
Applying the factors
* Private interest. Eldridge would receive full retroactive payment if he won, so his only interest was uninterrupted income in the meantime (at 340). The length of a wrongful deprivation matters (at 341). Here the delay exceeded a year, which the Court called significant (at 341–42). Still, because disability benefits are not need-based, the harm was less than in the welfare-benefits case where the Court did require a prior hearing (at 342–43).
* Risk of error. Disability decisions rest on "routine, standard, and unbiased medical reports," which are "sharply focused and easily documented." Credibility and veracity rarely matter, which lowers the value of a live hearing (at 343–44). Rules are set for "the generality of cases, not the rare exceptions" (at 344).
* Existing safeguards. Eldridge received notice of the tentative decision, the reasons for it, a summary of the evidence, full access to his file through a representative, and a chance to respond. That let him "mold" his argument to the issues that mattered (at 337–38, 345–46). A post-termination evidentiary hearing and judicial review were also available (at 339).
* Government interest. Cost alone does not control, but it must be weighed (at 347–48). The trial model is "neither a required, nor even the most effective" method in every setting (at 348). Officials charged by Congress with running the program get "substantial weight" for their good-faith procedural judgments (at 349).
Dissent (Brennan, joined by Marshall)
Brennan would have required a pre-termination evidentiary hearing. He called the majority's view that the harm was limited "speculative." Eldridge's family lost its home and furniture and was forced to sleep in one bed (at 349–50).
cases.Government:
* Due process is flexible, not a trial. Process need not be judicial-style (at 334, 348). Factor three expressly weighs "the function involved" (at 335), and national security sits at the top of that scale.
* Later process can suffice. Mathews accepted deprivation first, with a full hearing and judicial review afterward (at 349). Habeas, an appeal, and a promised trial supply that later process.
* Restricted access is permissible. Eldridge could not personally examine his own medical reports; only his representative could. The Court found that restriction "not significant" (at 338 n.18). That supports sealing the evidence while giving counsel access.
* Defer to the officials responsible. Their good-faith procedural judgments get "substantial weight" (at 349).
cases.Bronner:
* Liberty is far weightier than money. Mathews involved benefits recoverable "retroactive[ly]" (at 340). Imprisonment cannot be paid back. If a year's loss of income was significant (at 341–42), a year of detention weighs far more.
* He hasn't received even Eldridge's minimum. Eldridge got reasons, a summary of the evidence, access to his file, and a chance to respond before the deprivation (at 345–46). Bronner has had none of these; the evidence is sealed. The irreducible core is "notice of the case against him and opportunity to meet it" (at 348–49).
* The risk of error is high. Mathews found low risk because the evidence was "unbiased medical reports" (at 344). Bronner's case rests on an anonymous tip, undisclosed NSA intelligence, and disputed intent: exactly the credibility questions where hearings matter most (at 343–44).
* Timing matters. Twelve months is not "a meaningful time" (at 333). Mathews's own jurisdiction holding recognizes that some claims cannot wait (at 331).
* Deference requires a congressional charge. The "substantial weight" goes to officials "charged by Congress" (at 349). Congress never charged the executive with offshore detention of lawful residents.
quotes: "The fundamental requirement of due process is the opportunity to be heard 'at a meaningful time and in a meaningful manner.'" (at 333)
"[D]ue process is flexible and calls for such procedural protections as the particular situation demands." (at 334)
"the possible length of wrongful deprivation ... is an important factor in assessing the impact of official action on the private interests." (at 341)
"procedural due process rules are shaped by the risk of error inherent in the truth-finding process as applied to the generality of cases, not the rare exceptions." (at 344)
"The essence of due process is the requirement that 'a person in jeopardy of serious loss [be given] notice of the case against him and opportunity to meet it.'" (at 348–49)

cases.title: Hamdi v. Rumsfeld, 542 U.S. 507 (2004)
cases.meta:
There was no majority opinion. Justice O'Connor wrote a four-Justice plurality, joined by Chief Justice Rehnquist and Justices Kennedy and Breyer. Justice Souter, joined by Justice Ginsburg, concurred in part, dissented in part, and concurred in the judgment. Justice Scalia dissented, joined by Justice Stevens. Justice Thomas dissented alone. The Court decided the case June 28, 2004.
How the votes add up
* AUMF authorizes detention: 5 Justices (the plurality plus Thomas).
* Notice and a chance to rebut before a neutral decisionmaker as the minimum process: at least 6 (the plurality plus Souter and Ginsburg, at 553).
* Rejecting the government's position: 8 Justices (at 553).
cases.Facts:
Hamdi was born in Louisiana and moved to Saudi Arabia as a child. Northern Alliance forces seized him in Afghanistan in 2001 and turned him over to the U.S. military. He was held at Guantanamo, then moved to a Navy brig in Virginia in April 2002 once the military learned he was a citizen (at 510). The government claimed it could hold him indefinitely, without charges or proceedings (at 510–11).
His father filed a habeas petition, saying Hamdi had gone to Afghanistan to do relief work (at 511). The government's only evidence was the Mobbs Declaration, a hearsay affidavit by a Defense Department official (at 512–13). The District Court called it "little more than the government's 'say-so'" (at 513). The Fourth Circuit ordered the petition dismissed (at 514–16).
Questions
1. Is the Executive authorized to detain citizens who qualify as "enemy combatants" (at 516)?
2. What process is due to a citizen who disputes that status (at 524)?
cases.Holding:
The judgment was vacated and the case remanded. Congress authorized detention "in the narrow circumstances alleged." But a citizen held as an enemy combatant must receive "a meaningful opportunity to contest the factual basis for that detention before a neutral decisionmaker" (at 509).
Plurality (O'Connor)
Authority
* Narrow definition. The Court used the government's definition: a person "part of or supporting forces hostile to the United States" in Afghanistan who "engaged in an armed conflict against the United States" there. It answered "only the narrow question" (at 516).
* No ruling on Article II. The plurality did not reach whether Article II alone authorizes detention, because the AUMF did (at 516–17).
* Detention is incident to war. Detention "for the duration of the particular conflict" is a "fundamental and accepted an incident to war," and so is part of the authorized "necessary and appropriate force" (at 518). Its purpose is to prevent a return to the battlefield (at 518).
* Citizenship is no bar (at 519, relying on Quirin).
* Limits on duration and purpose. Indefinite detention for interrogation is not authorized. If a conflict is "entirely unlike" those that shaped the law of war, the authority "may unravel" (at 521). The war on terror is "broad and malleable," and perpetual detention is "not farfetched" (at 520).
* Milligan distinguished. Milligan was "a resident of Indiana arrested while at home there." Had he been captured carrying a rifle on a Confederate battlefield, the result "might well have been different" (at 522). The outer bounds of the enemy-combatant category are left to the lower courts (at 522 n.1).
* Status must be established first. Authority to detain exists only "once it is sufficiently clear that the individual is, in fact, an enemy combatant" (at 523).
* Location shouldn't control. Treating offshore detention differently would create a "perverse incentive" to keep citizen-detainees abroad (at 524).
Process
* Habeas. Absent suspension, habeas is available to every individual detained in the United States (at 525). The habeas statutes contemplate an opportunity to present and rebut facts (at 526).
* Mathews applies. The interest at stake is "the most elemental of liberty interests" (at 529). War or the nature of the accusation does not reduce that weight (at 530–31). The risk of error is "very real," and unchecked detention can become "a means for oppression" (at 530).
* The floor. "notice of the factual basis for his classification, and a fair opportunity to rebut the Government's factual assertions before a neutral decisionmaker," given "at a meaningful time and in a meaningful manner" (at 533).
* What can be tailored. Courts may accept hearsay and may presume the government's evidence correct, as long as the presumption is rebuttable (at 533–34). Initial battlefield captures need no hearing; the process attaches when the decision is made to continue detention (at 534).
* No blank check. "a state of war is not a blank check for the President" (at 536). The "some evidence" standard is inadequate (at 537), and an interrogation by one's captor is not a neutral proceeding (at 537).
* Who provides the process. A properly constituted military tribunal might suffice. Otherwise the habeas court "must itself ensure" the minimum (at 538). Hamdi also has a right to counsel (at 539).
Other opinions
Souter (with Ginsburg)
* No authorization. The Non-Detention Act requires clear congressional authorization to detain a citizen (at 543–44). Under the clear-statement rule, Congress is presumed to impose "no greater restraint on the citizen than was clearly and unmistakably indicated" (at 544).
* Wrong branch. The branch responsible for security should not be the one striking the balance with liberty (at 545).
* The AUMF falls short. It never uses the word "detention," and the criminal code already supplies a "well-stocked statutory arsenal," including material-support offenses (at 547–48).
* Congress limits alien detention. Thirty-eight days after the AUMF, Congress capped detention of suspected alien terrorists at seven days without charges or removal proceedings (at 551).
* Emergency power has limits. The Executive may be able to detain someone who is an imminent threat. But "an emergency power of necessity must at least be limited by the emergency" (at 552).
* Joins the judgment. He joined the remand and agreed with notice and a chance to rebut as the floor. He did not accept the burden-shifting presumption or the possibility that a military tribunal could cut off habeas review (at 553–54).
Scalia (with Stevens), dissenting
* Tradition: try or release. When the government accuses a citizen of waging war, the tradition is to prosecute; the alternative is for Congress to suspend the writ (at 554).
* Labels don't change the analysis. It is "unthinkable" that the Executive could make criminal grounds for detention noncriminal "merely by disclaiming an intent to prosecute" (at 556).
* History. The 1679 Habeas Corpus Act effectively limited untried detention to three to six months (at 557–58).
* Quirin's limits. Quirin rested on "conceded facts." Absent suspension, a citizen held where the courts are open gets "either ... criminal trial or ... a judicial decree requiring his release" (at 571–72).
* On Mathews. It is a disability-benefits case (at 575).
* Narrow scope. His view covers only citizens held within a federal court's jurisdiction. "Where the citizen is captured outside and held outside the United States, the constitutional requirements may be different." Detention is also lawful "once prosecution is in progress or in contemplation" (at 577).
Thomas, dissenting
* Defer to the political branches. The detention "falls squarely within the Federal Government's war powers," and courts "lack the expertise and capacity to second-guess that decision." War powers cannot be "balanced away" (at 579).
* Strongest presumption. The President acted with congressional authorization and gets "the strongest of presumptions." Courts are bound by the political branches' determination that the nation is at war, and detention power does not end with formal hostilities (at 588).
* Process received. Hamdi "received all the process to which he was due" (at 594).
cases.Government:
* Detention is authorized. Five Justices read the AUMF to authorize detention as a fundamental incident of war (at 518–19). NDAA § 1021 now says so expressly. If citizenship is no bar (at 519), lawful permanent residence is no bar either.
* The remedy is process, not release. Hamdi vacated and remanded for a hearing; it did not order release (at 509, 538). Bronner is in habeas now, so a habeas court can supply whatever process is due.
* Process can be tailored. Hamdi allows hearsay, a rebuttable presumption favoring the government, and summaries by a knowledgeable affiant (at 533–34). That accommodates sealed evidence.
* Detention abroad. Scalia reserved the question for persons held outside the United States (at 577). He also accepted detention while prosecution is "in contemplation" (at 577), and the government says it will try Bronner "as soon as practicable."
cases.Bronner:
* This is the Milligan case. The plurality distinguished Milligan because he was arrested at home in Indiana (at 522). Bronner was arrested at home in Olympus by the FBI. Hamdi's holding is limited to a battlefield capture in Afghanistan (at 516, 518).
* No inherent-power support. The plurality expressly did not reach Article II (at 516–17).
* The floor has not been met. Sealed evidence he has never seen means no notice. Twelve months without a hearing is not "a meaningful time." Executive assertions "simply presumed correct" fall "constitutionally short" (at 533, 537).
* The accusation doesn't lower the scale. The liberty interest is not reduced by the allegations or the war (at 530–31).
* Location doesn't matter. The plurality rejected a constitutional distinction based on offshore detention (at 524).
* Souter's points fit precisely. He is already charged with material support, the very "arsenal" Souter cited (at 547–48). Congress capped detention of alien terrorists at seven days (at 551). And any emergency is long over (at 552).
quotes: "a state of war is not a blank check for the President when it comes to the rights of the Nation's citizens." (at 536)
"notice of the factual basis for his classification, and a fair opportunity to rebut the Government's factual assertions before a neutral decisionmaker." (at 533)

"Any process in which the Executive's factual assertions go wholly unchallenged or are simply presumed correct without any opportunity for the alleged combatant to demonstrate otherwise falls constitutionally short." (at 537)
"indefinite detention for the purpose of interrogation is not authorized." (at 521)
"an emergency power of necessity must at least be limited by the emergency" (at 552, Souter, J.)

cases.title: Banyee v. Garland, 115 F.4th 928 (8th Cir. 2024)
cases.meta:
Judge Stras wrote for a unanimous panel (Benton, Grasz, Stras). The opinion was filed September 17, 2024, and rehearing en banc was denied. It is persuasive authority only.
Warning first. The Fourteenth Circuit dissent says Banyee "emphasized that even where statutes authorize detention, due process may require periodic review" (IC at 18). That is not what Banyee holds. Banyee reversed a district court that had ordered individualized review, and it rejected any multi-factor reasonableness test (at 931, 933). If you argue Bronner's side, do not adopt the dissent's characterization. Opposing counsel or the bench could just read you the opinion. The majority's description (IC at 13) is the accurate one.
cases.Facts:
Banyee, a citizen of Ivory Coast, grew up in the United States as a lawful permanent resident. As an adult he committed a series of crimes, the last of which was robbery with a dangerous weapon. That conviction triggered deportation proceedings (at 930). The proceedings went back and forth for years: the immigration judge first cancelled removal, the government won on appeal, and Banyee's own appeal remains pending (at 930).
Throughout, he was held under 8 U.S.C. § 1226(c), which mandates detention of certain criminal aliens (at 930). After a year in a county jail, the District Court applied a multi-factor "reasonableness" test. It ordered a bond hearing within 30 days, with the government bearing the burden of proving danger or flight risk by clear and convincing evidence. Banyee was released on bond (at 931).
cases.Question: Did a year-long mandatory detention pending deportation violate due process in the absence of an individualized hearing (at 931)?
cases.Holding: No. The court reversed and remanded for denial of the habeas petition (at 934). "Due process imposes no time limit on detention pending deportation" (at 930).
cases.Reasoning:
* Settled rule. Detention during deportation proceedings is constitutional. "Congress may make rules as to aliens that would be unacceptable if applied to citizens" (at 931, quoting Supreme Court precedent).
* No individualized findings required. The government may detain "by reference to the legislative scheme," without showing that the particular person is dangerous (at 931–32).
* Purpose, not length. "Nothing suggests that length determines legality." What matters is that detention has "a definite termination point," either deportation or release. That makes it "materially different" from "potentially permanent" confinement. "The why ... is more important than how long" (at 932).
* The limits. Detention used to punish aliens who have not been convicted of a crime is unconstitutional (at 932–33). So is detention when deportation is only "a remote possibility," or when unreasonable delay shows the person is held "for other reasons" (at 933).
* No Mathews balancing here. Mathews ordinarily governs, but the Supreme Court "ha[s] already done whatever balancing is necessary" in this setting and adopted a bright-line rule: detention is permitted while proceedings remain "pending" (at 933).
* Application. Banyee's proceedings were still pending and deportation remained possible (at 933–34). He also "has the keys in his pocket": he could end detention by dropping his defense and leaving (at 933). There was no sign the proceedings were "a ruse," because the delay came from hard legal questions and backlog, not "dilatory tactics" by either side (at 934). Housing him in a jail with criminal inmates did not convert detention into punishment (at 934).
cases.Government:
* Twelve months is not dispositive. Banyee was held a year, and the court said length does not determine legality (at 930, 932).
* No individualized hearing is required. The court rejected a hearing on dangerousness and a reasonableness test (at 931–33). The majority below relies on exactly this (IC at 13).
* Aliens get different rules. Congress may treat aliens in ways "unacceptable if applied to citizens" (at 931). Bronner is a lawful permanent resident, not a citizen. Banyee was too.
* A definite end point exists. Bronner's detention ends at trial, which the government says will come "as soon as practicable." That is not "potentially permanent" confinement (at 932).
* Jail conditions don't make detention punishment (at 934).
cases.Bronner:
* Banyee's own test cuts against the government. Banyee's detention served a specific purpose: carrying out a pending deportation (at 932). Bronner is in no removal proceeding and has no removal order. What legitimate purpose does offshore military custody serve? Detention without that purpose is the punishment Banyee says is unconstitutional (at 932–33).
* No definite end point. NDAA § 1021(c)(1) allows detention "until the end of the hostilities," which is the "potentially permanent" confinement Banyee distinguishes (at 932; App. III).
* This looks like the "ruse" exception. Banyee's delay came from neutral causes; neither side was dilatory (at 934). Bronner's delay comes from the government's own choice to seal its evidence. The government also abandoned a pending federal prosecution in favor of military custody. That suggests he is held "for other reasons" (at 933–34).
* The statute mattered. Banyee upheld detention that Congress mandated in § 1226(c), defended "by reference to the legislative scheme" (at 930, 932). ATA § 4(b)(1) authorizes offshore detention only for persons unlawfully present, so Bronner's detention lacks that statutory footing.
* No keys in his pocket. Banyee could end his detention by leaving the country (at 933). Bronner cannot.
* Status rested on convictions. Banyee was deportable because of actual convictions (at 930). Bronner was reclassified on an accusation alone.

"'[D]ue process,' unlike some legal rules, is not a technical conception with a fixed content unrelated to time, place and circumstances." Cafeteria Workers v. McElroy, 367 U.S. 886, 895 (1961).
"[D]ue process is flexible and calls for such procedural protections as the particular situation demands." Morrissey v. Brewer, 408 U.S. 471, 481 (1972).

"The essence of due process is the requirement that 'a person in jeopardy of serious loss [be given] notice of the case against him and opportunity to meet it.'" Joint Anti-Fascist Comm. v. McGrath, 341 U.S. 123, 171-172 (1951) (Frankfurter, J., concurring).

"For more than a century the central meaning of procedural due process has been clear: 'Parties whose rights are to be affected are entitled to be heard; and in order that they may enjoy that right they must first be notified.' It is equally fundamental that the right to notice and an opportunity to be heard 'must be granted at a meaningful time and in a meaningful manner.'" Fuentes v. Shevin, 407 U.S. 67, 80 (1972).

That even purportedly fair adjudicators "are disqualified by their interest in the controversy to be decided is, of course, the general rule." Tumey v. Ohio, 273 U.S. 510, 522 (1927).

Carey v. Piphus, 435 U.S. 247, 259 (1978) ("Procedural due process rules are meant to protect persons not from the deprivation, but from the mistaken or unjustified deprivation of life, liberty, or property"); id. at 266 ("the right to procedural due process is 'absolute' in the sense that it does not depend upon the merits of a claimant's substantive assertions").

Where "issues of witness credibility and veracity often are critical to the decisionmaking process," "written submissions are a wholly unsatisfactory basis for decision." Goldberg v. Kelly, 397 U.S. 254, 269 (1970).

Differences in the origin and function of administrative agencies "preclude wholesale transplantation of the rules of procedure, trial, and review which have evolved from the history and experience of courts." FCC v. Pottsville Broadcasting Co., 309 U.S. 134, 143 (1940).

Kim, 538 U.S. 510, 527 (2003) ("detention ... d[oes] not serve its purported immigration purpose" when deportation is no longer an option).
